record.title: Production database-agent losses often follow tool use, and server defects move model scores
record.summary: The authors analyze 8,199 runs over eleven days from an open-source SQL client’s agent mode, covering 39 locally served open-weight models and one hosted control across six task surfaces. They report that 1,590 of 2,100 model-attributed losses (75.7%) occurred after at least one tool call; the majority persists in 99.7% of model-clustered resamples. Five server-side changes, without model or prompt changes, moved six selected models by 6–21 cells out of 30. The paper cautions that its transport/clock/verification/capability loss-class ordering is specific to this corpus and does not generalize.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In an 11-day production corpus of 8,199 runs, the authors attribute 2,100 agent-mode losses to named models; 1,590 (75.7%) followed at least one tool call. The majority persisted in 99.7% of clustered resamples over models.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that five server-side interventions, changing no model, prompt or sampling setting, moved six selected models by 6–21 cells out of 30.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports a context-memory confound in which an uncapped 7.1 GB model loaded a 262,144-token context and held 51 GB on a 64 GB machine, producing runs that ordinary logs could misclassify as model timeouts.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent group has audited the released corpus/scorer or reproduced the failure decomposition and server interventions.
The study covers one SQL client product; authors are contributors to the evaluated software. Transfer to other tools, tasks and server contracts is unknown.
Before/after readings were selected from low-scoring/open cells and use 30 runs per model; the paper explicitly warns these are field observations, not an effect-size estimate.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated across production agent systems, the reported loss decomposition and server-side fixes could materially change how teams diagnose model capability, design tool contracts and allocate engineering effort. Evidence currently comes from one product and a contributor-authored study with selected intervention comparisons.
limitations: Single-product production corpus (LibreDB Studio) and six task surfaces; external generalization is unestablished.
Authors are contributors to the evaluated software. The paper releases artifacts, but this does not constitute independent replication.
Loss-class ordering varies under model-clustered resampling and is described by the authors as a property of this corpus rather than a general result.
The six before/after model readings were selected from open low-scoring cells and have only 30 runs each; authors report them as field observations, not effect-size estimates.

The paper identifies earlier work on tool-feedback and harness-mediated failures; its contribution is production-scale evidence and server-side diagnostic/intervention detail, not discovery that harnesses can matter.
brief.summary: The authors analyze 8,199 runs over eleven days from an open-source SQL client’s agent mode, covering 39 locally served open-weight models and one hosted control across six task surfaces. They report that 1,590 of 2,100 model-attributed losses (75.7%) occurred after at least one tool call; the majority persists in 99.7% of model-clustered resamples. Five server-side changes, without model or prompt changes, moved six selected models by 6–21 cells out of 30. The paper cautions that its transport/clock/verification/capability loss-class ordering is specific to this corpus and does not generalize.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 1,590 of 2,100 model-attributed losses followed tool use in one 8,199-run production corpus, with the majority robust to model-clustered resampling; five server changes moved six selected models by 6–21/30 cells.
technical.demonstrated_result: the research desk did not independently demonstrate the paper’s results. The authors report a production corpus and five server-side changes associated with improved scores in six selected model/task cells.
technical.mechanism: Instrument the complete agent loop, including tool-call arguments and server refusals, to distinguish model non-engagement from transport/schema/verification failures; correct server-side tool-contract defects without changing model weights or prompts.
technical.regime: Eleven days of agent mode in the LibreDB Studio open-source SQL client; 39 open-weight models served locally and one hosted control; six database task surfaces; 8,199 total runs and 110,711 ledger events.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links corpus, scorer, verifier and tool-call argument captures. the research desk inspected the text and artifact listing but did not independently execute the verifier or reproduce the intervention effects.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the paper, pre-intervention runs on the same hardware, prompts and tasks are compared with selected post-intervention readings. These before/after cells were selected from low-scoring open cases and are not a randomized causal estimate.

brief.title: Production database-agent losses often follow tool use, and server defects move model scores
brief.why_it_matters: If the result transfers, tool-agent failures can be misattributed to model capability when interface and server defects are the binding cause; fixing one harness defect may improve several models at once. The paper is a single-product production study by contributors to the evaluated software, and its selected intervention readings do not establish general effect sizes.
